source.text:
Hey man, do whatever you want! I'm just some guy giving out free analysis of how the world is on the internet.

> The industrial revolution wasn't based upon, to quote Brent Hecht, a Director of Applied Science at Microsoft, “the greatest theft of labor in human history”.

It's probably true but I suspect we're past the point of putting the genie back in the bottle. People are free to try though! I don't love it myself, but I don't see an overwhelming enough majority of people against it.

> One extra thing that you don't seem to be considering at all is that the need for developers, like designers and a number of other jobs, has a good chance of falling considerably.

I hear what you're saying here, and that's part of the reason I argue for going as far down the value chain as possible. If you own land and can do some farming to feed yourself and generate your own power with solar and don't need to buy much fuel then you're not immune to the wider economy, but you're pretty well insulated from it. If you could survive for 3mo without a salary that's great but you're still pretty fragile to a temporary disruption. But if you could survive 3 years without a salary? Now you have some real breathing space.

> WRT “we won't know for a long time” - are you suggesting that while we don't know either way, we should all go one way instead of the other?

Not even close, I'm just saying that when a big societal change happens it takes society a long time to digest it and for a new kind of order to emerge.

200 years on from the steam engine and 100 years on from electrification and 90% or more of the people in the developed world have opted-in to that system. Enough so that we have words for those who didn't because they're so different. Is that good or bad? It's kind of irrelevant for the discussion. What matters is if you think the impact will be as big. If so, you need to think big thoughts about how it plays out. If not? You just make some minor tactical adjustments and get on with life.

> That is going off at the deep end… There is a vast difference between not directly using it myself and not touching anything that it has ever touched.

How do you plan to accurately predict how far the deployment will go and how you will avoid it? This isn't a "gotcha" question, I'm honestly looking for answers myself. Manual labor will avoid immediate encroachment for sure, but people are working on robots too, of all shapes and sizes. I'm struggling to think of some industry that I can confidently predict will be largely immune to automation.

I suppose the unionized trades will probably fend automation off for a while because the environments are so dynamic. A plumber or electrician won't immediately become obsolete as not every detail of every house in the world is mapped and the cost of doing so isn't obviously amortizable. But even there as the costs of mapping go down so do the moats shrink. Would some company give away below-cost robot lawn mowing service to get better data? It's possible.

I'd love to hear your thoughts on the industries that seem less vulnerable to AI-ification.
